st.headline: Keppel, Starhub discuss M1 deal; Grab execs buy shares after stock falls: Markets this week
st.teaser: The STI closed higher on Sept 25 at 5,710.65 despite uncertainty over Trump-Xi talks and a jump in US Treasury yields.
fullText: SINGAPORE – Singapore stocks ended the week slightly higher despite a cautious mood around Chinese President Xi Jinping’s Sept 23-25 US state visit with President Donald Trump, where disputes over tariffs and artificial intelligence remained unresolved.

The Straits Times Index rose 27.28 points, or 0.48 per cent, from its Sept 18 close to finish at 5,710.65 on Sept 25. It had climbed to 5,723.76 on Sept 22, but gave up some of those gains as a sell-off in US government bonds pushed yields higher.

Saxo UK investor strategist Neil Wilson noted “aggressive unloading” of US bonds on Sept 24, as the 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.23 per cent, a 19-year high, and the 30-year yield rose above 5.5 per cent, its highest level since 2004.
Yields had eased by Sept 25, but remained elevated: US Treasury data put the 10-year yield at 5.17 per cent and the 30-year yield at 5.49 per cent. Bond yields rise when their prices fall.
With inflation still above the Federal Reserve’s 2 per cent target, investors were also weighing the prospect of another quarter-point interest rate increase by the US central bank in October.

In Singapore, the three local banks outperformed the broader market over the week. Compared with their Sept 18 closes, DBS gained 1.43 per cent to end at $78, OCBC rose 1.88 per cent to $32.01 and UOB added 1.87 per cent to $42.57.
Listed companies will be held to higher standards of transparency and shareholder communication from Jan 1, 2027.

Among the new obligations rolled out by the Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo) on Sept 23, every listed firm must have a dedicated investor relations policy published on its company website to facilitate regular, effective and fair communication with shareholders.
At a minimum, it must set out the channels through which the issuer communicates with investors, including the mechanisms by which investors may contact the issuer.
Companies are also encouraged to publish their annual reports, minutes of annual general meetings, investor presentation decks and a calendar of upcoming events on their websites.

Annual reports must include a link to the company’s investor relations policy, a description of its dividend policy, and a description of key shareholder engagement activities within the year. While companies are not required to issue dividends, they must explain their reasons for not doing so if they choose not to.
Listed companies must also clearly explain the factors used to determine the amount paid to the company’s executive directors and executives, including the chief executive, in their annual reports.
The new rules are to “target specific communication gaps and are aimed at elevating disclosure quality”, said the regulator.
StarHub and Keppel, in bourse filings on Sept 23, confirmed that they were discussing a potential deal involving telco M1.
Keppel, which owns a majority stake in M1, said it continues to explore consolidation opportunities involving M1, as it believes consolidation “is needed for Singapore’s telco sector”.
Should a deal materialise between Starhub and M1, it would reduce the number of mobile network operators in Singapore from four to three, subject to regulatory approval.
Shares for StarHub climbed during the week, reaching a peak of $1.15 on Sept 24 before closing on Sept 25 at $1.12.
Keppel shares also rose, peaking at $11.45 on Sept 24. The shares closed the week on Sept 25 at $11.30.

M1’s telco business returned to the spotlight after Simba’s proposed $1.4 billion takeover fell through in May. The Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) had suspended its assessment of the deal while investigating Simba’s unauthorised use of radio frequency bands that it was not assigned to provide mobile services.
Simba said earlier on Sept 23 that it had used frequency spectrum beyond the limits permitted by the regulator.

“There was some use of spectrum that was permitted by the IMDA, and we then used it outside the limitations that were in that purpose,” said Tony Moffatt, company secretary of Simba’s Australian-listed parent Tuas, in an earnings call.

Grab shares rose 8.9 per cent on Sept 22 after CEO Anthony Tan bought about US$30 million (S$38.3 million) worth of shares and president Alex Hungate purchased about US$867,000 worth of shares the previous day, according to US regulatory filings.

Grab shares had fallen to a three-year low of US$2.74 on Sept 18, after the company on Sept 15 announced a US$1.49 billion deal to acquire a 60 per cent stake in buy-now-pay-later provider Atome Financial.
It will acquire the remaining 40 per cent around two years after the first stage of the deal is completed, which is expected to be in the third quarter of 2027, subject to certain conditions.

The deal, which Grab said would give the ride-hailing giant a ready-made consumer-lending operation to complement its existing mix of financial services, could ultimately value Atome at up to US$4.5 billion, a sum some analysts have said may be too much to pay for synergies that have yet to be demonstrated.
At a company town hall, Tan was reported to have said: “I have put my money where my mouth is... I believe in our strategy and our direction.”
Grab closed Sept 25 at US$3.13, up 10.6 per cent through the week.
Seatrium on Sept 22 launched a new $200 million share buyback programme after fully using its previous $100 million allocation on Sept 1.

Seatrium CEO Chris Ong said the larger buyback reflects a clear pathway for future growth underpinned by strengthened fundamentals and margins, and a robust global pipeline of offshore and marine work. He added that it would continue to allocate capital carefully while returning cash to shareholders.

The new buyback programme will be done progressively, funded by existing cash resources and repurchases of up to a maximum of 2 per cent of its total issued shares. The buyback will be subject to shareholder approval at each annual general meeting.

cna.headline: RSAF moving to new runway as part of Paya Lebar Air Base relocation plans
cna.teaser: Then-Defence Minister Ng Eng Hen said in 2015 that Changi Air Base East would have to be expanded to replace Paya Lebar Air Base.
fullText: SINGAPORE: The Republic of Singapore Air Force (RSAF) will be moving to a new runway as part of plans to relocate Paya Lebar Air Base from 2030 and beyond, the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) said on Saturday (Sep 26).
In response to CNA's query, a ministry spokesperson said the RSAF will be shifting its operations from its current runway, known as 02R/20L, to a new runway 03/21, at Changi Air Base East.
Then-Defence Minister Ng Eng Hen had said in 2015 that Changi Air Base East and Tengah Air Base would have to be expanded to accommodate various assets and facilities to replace Paya Lebar Air Base.

He said then that the focus was on expanding the Changi Air Base East and building a new runway, adding that it was a complex undertaking that required highly skilled engineering and close coordination with the ongoing runway and terminal expansion works at Changi Airport.
According to the document, the new runway would be operational from Sep 17, 2026 and would not be available for civilian use.
Current Defence Minister Chan Chun Sing said in September 2025 that the planned relocation of Paya Lebar Air Base remained on track for 2030 and beyond.
In his parliamentary reply, he reiterated that the relocation of an air base was complex and that it would be done progressively as essential aircraft support infrastructure becomes ready.
He had been asked whether there were plans to progressively reduce the frequency of flights from Paya Lebar Air Base leading up to its decommissioning in 2030.
The frequency of flights from Paya Lebar Air Base will be reduced progressively during the relocation phase, Mr Chan said.
Paya Lebar Air Base's relocation was first announced during the National Day Rally 2013 by then-Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong.
He said the move would free up an area of about 800ha – bigger than Bishan or Ang Mo Kio – which could be used to build new homes, offices, factories, parks, living environments and communities.

listening.title: Singapore's LTA Reverses Plan to Phase Out Classic Ez-Link Cards
listening.transcript: Following widespread public feedback, the Land Transport Authority has decided to shelf its plans to phase out older ez-link cards. Many commuters, especially seniors, voiced concerns about not being able to see their card balances at MRT fare gates. This swift policy pivot highlights the challenges of balancing technological advancement with inclusivity in Singapore's rapidly ageing society.

economistArticle.title: The Battle for India's Bourses: A Duopoly Reheated
paras: The duopoly governing India’s financial markets is entering a turbulent new chapter. For years, the National Stock Exchange (NSE) has reigned supreme, dominating the highly lucrative derivatives segment and leaving its older sibling, the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE), in the shadows. However, a series of strategic maneuvers by BSE’s aggressive new leadership has successfully reignited a fierce turf war.

BSE, Asia's oldest bourse, has successfully revitalized its weekly options contracts. By slashing transaction fees and restructuring expiry dates to avoid direct clashes with the NSE, BSE has clawed back lost market share. Retail investors, attracted by cheaper trading costs and high volatility, are flocking to the revived products, forcing the market leader to defend its turf with equal vigor.

This corporate clash extends beyond mere pricing strategies; it is a battle for technological supremacy. While NSE has historically boasted superior throughput and lower latency, BSE has invested heavily in upgrading its trading architecture to process millions of orders seamlessly. The stakes are immense, as India's retail trading boom shows no signs of cooling down, fueled by millions of tech-savvy youths entering the market via smartphone apps.

Regulators are keeping a watchful eye on this escalating rivalry. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) is particularly concerned about the systemic risks posed by retail investors piling into speculative options trading. While competition breeds efficiency and lowers costs for market participants, it also risks inflating a speculative bubble that could burst spectacularly.

Ultimately, the renewed competition between BSE and NSE is a healthy sign of a maturing financial ecosystem. As both giants vie for dominance, they will drive innovations in financial products and risk management. For global investors looking at India as a primary growth engine, this rivalry promises a more robust, liquid, and dynamic market landscape.
economistArticle.cn:
主导印度金融市场的双头垄断格局正在进入一个动荡的新篇章。多年来，国家证券交易所（NSE）一直称霸市场，在极具吸引力的衍生品领域占据主导地位，将历史更悠久的孟买证券交易所（BSE）甩在阴影之中。然而，BSE具有进取心的新管理层采取了一系列战略举措，成功重新点燃了一场激烈的地盘之争。

作为亚洲最古老的交易所，BSE成功重振了其周度期权合约。通过大幅削减交易费用并重新调整到期日以避免与NSE正面交锋，BSE已经夺回了失去的市场份额。在更便宜的交易成本和高波动的吸引下，散户投资者纷纷涌向这些重获新生的产品，迫使市场领头羊不得不以同样的力度保卫自己的地盘。

这场企业冲突不仅局限于定价策略，更是一场技术霸权的争夺。虽然NSE在历史上一直以卓越的吞吐量和更低的延迟引以为豪，但BSE已投入巨资升级其交易架构，以无缝处理数百万笔订单。由于在智能手机应用推动下，数百万熟悉科技的年轻人涌入市场，印度的散户交易热潮毫无降温迹象，因此这场争夺的赌注巨大。

监管机构正密切关注这场升级的竞争。印度证券交易委员会（SEBI）尤其担心散户盲目涌入投机性期权交易带来的系统性风险。虽然竞争能带来效率并降低市场参与者的成本，但也存在吹大投机泡沫的风险，而这种泡沫可能会以惨烈的方式破裂。

归根结底，BSE与NSE之间重新燃起的竞争是金融生态系统走向成熟的健康迹象。随着这两大巨头争夺霸主地位，它们将推动金融产品和风险管理的创新。对于将印度视为主要增长引擎的全球投资者而言，这场竞争预示着一个更具韧性、流动性更强且更具活力的市场格局。

This structure is highly effective in professional and analytical writing. / 这句话巧妙地使用了让步连词 'While' 来呈现平衡的观点，对比了眼前的利益（效率提升、成本降低）与长期的系统性风险（投机泡沫破裂）。这种结构在专业和分析性写作中非常具有说服力。
